newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Jan 6.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Jan 6.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- MAJOR ACTS TO HEAD OFF NEW BATTLE ON EUROPE

Despite a continuing apparent shift towards Euroscepticism by his cabinet, John Major over the weekend stressed that there would be no change in his determination to keep Britain's options open on whether it eventually joins the planned single European currency. Last week Stephen Dorrell, health secretary, called for a fundamental review of EU policy, prompting speculation that he might challenge for the party leadership.
-- VALUE OF TELECOMS DEALS DOUBLES TO 81 BILLION STG

Figures compiled by the Financial Times reveal that 1996 saw a doubling to 80.8 billion stg in the value of mergers, acquisitions and privatisations in the telecoms industry worldwide. It is anticipated that with the number of share offerings already planned for 1997 that this trend in the sector will continue. Already planning privatisations during the forthcoming 12 months are Telefonica, France Telecom, Stet and Telstra. The largest number of takeovers took place in 1996 in the US market, where local companies have been reacting to the liberalisation of the market.
-- BA 'WILL NOT BECOME VIRTUAL AIRLINE'

In a New Year message to staff the chief executive of British Airways has denied that the company is planning to outsource all traditional functions of an airline, with the exception of marketing. Speculation that this course of action was planned was triggered after the company made it clear that it intended to make savings of one billion sterling a year over three years. Although it plans to contract certain functions, such as baggage handling, some have suggested that the policy could be expanded to include the flying of its planes.
-- DEMAND FOR COMMERCIAL PROPERTY ACCELERATING

A survey published by the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) on Monday reveals that an increasing number of UK companies are planning to raise their holdings of commercial property. The appetite for such property is based on an increase in the strength of the domestic market and the expectation that this trend will continue. The survey has also found that companies are once more showing interest in acquiring a presence in town centres.
-- TELEPHONE FRAUD 'INCREASING RAPIDLY'

An organisation representing telecommunications managers, the TMA, alleges that as few as 35 people could be responsible for most of the 100,000 cases of telephone fraud each year in Britain. It is believed that the cost of such crime in the UK currently runs at some 200 million stg annually and that the problem is set to increase further. The TMA is calling for greater efforts to be made by both regulators and telecoms companies to alert users to the threat of fraud and develop preventative systems.
-- EMPLOYERS WARNED ON ATTITUDE TO SKILLS

A report from the Department of Education and Employment warns that in order to remain competitive on a global level, British businesses will have to reassess their attitude to employee training. Although the labour market has become a great deal more flexible, workers are not being provided with the basic skills that will allow them to remain employable in an increasingly technology-dominated market. Employers are taking a shorter-term view on training, opting for a strategy that provides more immediate returns from staff who are likely to leave after a relatively short time.
-- NCR TO SUPPLY 30 MILLION POUND SYSTEM FOR REUTERS DATA

It is reported that NCR, the demerged computer unit of US telecoms giant AT&T, is to provide Reuters with some 30 million stg worth of equipment that will be used to develop advanced data warehousing capabilities. The Reuters data centre in London is to house the warehouse, which will allow users to intelligently search and retrieve information from a vast array of data. The data warehousing will be used in conjunction with a new range of information products from Reuters called the 3000 series.
-- TUC WARNINGS ON HOLIDAYS

The Trades Union Congress has warned that if Britain is allowed to opt-out from the EU's working time directive as many as 6 million workers will lose out on entitlement to paid holidays. Meanwhile, the Institute of Directors has warned that adoption of this directive as well as the social chapter could result in job creation in the UK being hampered. A survey of members found that just 3 percent believed that the working time directive could improve the way in which they operate.
-- LIFE ASSURERS POISED TO CUT SHORT-TERM BONUSES

It is reported that a number of life assurance companies are preparing to reduce the bonuses they pay out on short-term policies due to mature during the forthcoming year. Some 250,000 customers are expected to see policies mature in 1997. The average return on some of these policies is expected to be in the region of 4 percent to 5 percent -- a figure well down on that for last year. This will be the fifth year in which downward adjustments have had to be made.
